title: Post-January 6th deplatforming reduced the reach of misinformation on Twitter
screen_reason: Behavioural panel study of 599,697 US Twitter users matched to a voter file. Although the paper's AIM is a causal evaluation of deplatforming (an intervention-effect design, which on its own would be excluded), it reports descriptive quantitative shares with denominators in its sample description: the share of panellists who shared at least one misinformation URL (7.46%), and the share of all misinformation URLs shared that was contributed by the 0.23% of panellists who were deplatformed (24.13%). Those descriptive shares make it eligible under the rule that a study whose aim is something else is still included if a descriptive share is reported anywhere.

estimates.denominator: 599,697 active US Twitter users in the voter-file-matched panel who shared at least one URL of any kind between 30 June 2020 and 31 January 2021

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Combined domain list: the fake-news site list from Grinberg et al. (Science 2019) plus NewsGuard's proprietary list using the 29 March 2021 snapshot, with a score below 60 flagging a low-credibility domain; robustness checks with the Grinberg list alone, the NewsGuard list alone and Indiana University's Iffy list. No human content coding and no inter-coder reliability reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: We limit the analysis to active users matched to the US voter file. We define an active user as anyone who shared (via tweet or retweet) one URL during the 2020 election cycle between 30 June 2020 and 31 January 2021. There are 599,697 active users in our panel under this definition, who tweeted more than 8 million URLs during the study period.
estimates.notes: 44,743/599,697 = 7.46%, consistent with the stated percentage. The Methods give a very slightly different count for the same quantity ('there are 44,734 such users'), a one-digit discrepancy in the paper itself; the main-text figure with the percentage is used here. The paper elsewhere says 'only about 10% of the panellists share misinformation URLs' — an approximation that is not consistent with 7.46% and is not extracted (R8). Coded SHARING/actor_share per the instruction's explicit definition ('actor_share = % of users who shared any'); an adjudicator could argue for REACH/reach_subtype=sharing since the denominator is people reached-by-own-behaviour, but the instruction assigns this exact wording to SHARING.

estimates.page_loc: Methods, 'Subgroups' (also stated in main text 'Data', p. 136: 'These deplatformed users accounted for 4.35% of all URL sharing and 24.13% of all misinformation URLs shared among our sample during December 2020.')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same combined domain list (Grinberg et al. plus NewsGuard below 60, 29 March 2021 snapshot). Deplatformed status determined by Twitter API error codes on a profile snapshot collected 14-27 January 2021, cross-referenced with Abilov et al.'s VoterFraud2020 list of suspended voter-fraud accounts.
estimates.moderator_quote: We define a user as deplatformed if they were active prior to the intervention and suspended at the time we snapshotted their user profile on or after 14 January 2021.
estimates.notes: borderline=true because the concentrated group is defined by Twitter's enforcement action (deplatformed), not by a rank cut of the sharing distribution; it is nonetheless a stated small share of users (0.23%) accounting for a stated large share of misinformation sharing (24.13%), so it satisfies R1 (both conc_group_pct and conc_share_pct present verbatim). The companion figure '4.35% of all URL sharing' is the same group's share of ALL content, not of misinformation, so it is not extracted as a separate row.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Fig. 1 plots the daily percentage of posts containing a misinformation URL among all URL-containing tweets/retweets for the 2016 and 2020 cycles (y-axis 0-12.5%), which would be a SHARING content_share row, but no numeric point value is stated anywhere in the text — only 'the misinformation URL sharing rate among all users was five times higher in 2020 than in 2016' and 'the rate declined by about 50%', which are ratios/approximations, not shares (R8). Not extracted. (2) Supersharers are defined as 'the top 0.1% of the distribution of misinformation sharing', but the paper never states the share of misinformation sharing this group accounts for, so R1 is not met and no CONCENTRATION row is possible; the sentence '1% supersharers account for 0.1% of the sample' appears to be a typographical error in the paper. (3) QAnon users '0.16% of the panel' and followers '26.4%' of non-deplatformed users are group-size statistics, not misinformation shares. (4) All SRD/DID treatment effects (e.g. -1,726.4 retweets, 30% reduction, 5% increase) are causal estimates and changes, not prevalence shares, and are not extracted. (5) Absolute retweet counts (154, 162, 2,287, 1,607 per period) are counts without a misinformation-share denominator.

rob.design: Observational panel: 1.5 million Twitter accounts linked to a commercial US voter file (Grinberg et al./Hughes et al. panel), of which 599,697 were active URL-sharers during the 2020 election cycle (30 June 2020 - 31 January 2021); all tweets and retweets collected regularly since late 2017 (3 billion tweets to 12 July 2021). No response rate applies (behavioural trace data). Misinformation coded automatically at the domain level after URL redirect resolution, against the Grinberg et al. fake-news list plus NewsGuard (score <60, 29 March 2021 snapshot); no human coding and therefore no inter-coder reliability statistic; robustness reported against the Grinberg list alone, NewsGuard alone and the Iffy list. Known limitation stated by the authors: data collection was not real-time, so tweets deleted quickly may be missing, and collection frequency varies by user activity tier (daily for the 10,000 most active, weekly for the next 500,000, biweekly thereafter). Non-human accounts (bots, organisations) and pseudonymous users are excluded by the voter-file matching.
rob.item6_quote: Our domain list includes the list of 'fake news' sites from Grinberg et al.8, which operationalizes "sites that lack editorial norms and processes to ensure the credibility of information."
rob.item10_quote: A total of 44,743 users (7.46% of the full panel) were misinformation sharers (users who shared at least one misinformation URL during the 2020 election cycle), which is the subset of interest for our SRD and DID analyses.
